sentences.text: This giant dinosaur measured between 18 and 22 meters in length, with the subadult holotype weighing between 28.3 and 46.9 metric tons.
It possessed a disproportionately long neck, a small skull, and a massive overall body size.
Its front legs were longer than its hind legs, and it had a relatively shorter tail compared to its neck, distinguishing it from most other Jurassic sauropods.
The genus was first described by Elmer S. Riggs in 1903.
The original fossils were discovered in the Colorado River valley within western Colorado, United States.
The type species for this genus is Brachiosaurus altithorax.
Scientists regard this animal as a high browser capable of reaching vegetation up to 9 meters off the ground.
Unlike many other sauropods, this creature was not built to stand upright on its hind legs.
Recent studies suggest it was likely endothermic, or warm-blooded, challenging earlier ideas that linked its size to cold-bloodedness.
This genus serves as the namesake for the family Brachiosauridae.
A 2013 analysis proposed that remains labeled as B. nougaredi might actually belong to more than one species due to their wide geographic separation.
Metacarpals discovered in Algeria were determined to belong to an indeterminate titanosauriform rather than this specific genus.
This animal lived during the Late Jurassic period, spanning the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages.
It inhabited what is now North America approximately 154 to 153 million years ago.
Most size estimates for this genus are actually derived from the African species Giraffatitan brancai because more complete material exists for that animal.
There is ongoing discussion regarding whether this dinosaur was ectothermic or warm-blooded, though recent evidence points toward the latter.
In 2019, researchers raised questions about the classification of two specific specimens into their respective evolutionary groups.
Some scientists suggested that assigning the juvenile specimen nicknamed Toni to B. altithorax might rely on mistaken interpretations.
In 2009, Taylor proposed skeleton SII as the lectotype without realizing Janensch had previously designated SI.
